s: The work studies privacy risks in retrieval-augmented generation and its effects on large language models. It presents empirical studies and novel attack methods showing that RAG systems can leak information from a private retrieval database. It also finds that retrieval-augmented generation can mitigate leakage of large language models’ training data. These findings provide insights for privacy protection of retrieval-augmented LLMs and for builders of large language models and RAG systems.

l: The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), 1 / Introduction
s: This unit explains how retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combines retrieval from an external database with large language model (LLM) generation, and examines privacy risks in both sources of information. It asks whether private data can be extracted from the retrieval database and whether retrieval data affects LLM memorization. The authors propose a composite structured prompting attack and report that Llama2-7b-Chat and GPT-3.5-turbo can output verbatim or highly similar retrieval records at rates near 50% in their medical dialogue study. They also find that retrieval augmentation can substantially reduce the tendency of LLMs to output memorized training data.

l: The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), 2 / Related Work / 2.1 / Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) .. 2.2 / Privacy Risk of Large Language Models
s: Lewis et al. (2020) introduced retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which combines a dataset, retriever, and large language model to improve generation accuracy and relevance. RAG can mitigate hallucinations and supports flexible updates without retraining or fine-tuning the entire system, enabling applications such as personal chatbots and medical diagnostic assistants. Research on large language models shows that they can memorize and reveal information from pre-training corpora, with risks influenced by model size, data duplication, and prompt length. Studies also examine privacy risks in fine-tuning data and retrieval-based kNN-LM, although kNN-LM differs from RAG in architecture and mechanism.

s: Lewis et al. (2020) introduced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as an approach for enhancing large language model generation. It combines a dataset, retriever, and language model, whose components can be exchanged or updated without retraining or fine-tuning the entire system, and it is used in applications including personal chatbots and medical diagnostic assistants.

l: The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), 4 / RQ1: Can we extract private data from / 4.1 / Evaluation Setup .. 4.5 / Potential Mitigation
s: This unit evaluates privacy leakage from the external retrieval database in RAG using targeted and untargeted attacks. Experiments use the Enron Email dataset and HealthcareMagic-101 dataset with Llama-7b-chat, Llama-13b-chat, and GPT-3.5-turbo, finding that models can reproduce retrieved text and extract sensitive information. Ablations show that command design affects leakage, while increasing the number of retrieved documents produces only limited additional leakage. Re-ranking has little mitigation effect, summarization reduces untargeted leakage but can remain ineffective for targeted attacks, and distance thresholds create a privacy-utility tradeoff.

s: The evaluation finds substantial privacy leakage from retrieval data, including exact or similar text reproduction and extraction of targeted sensitive information. Leakage is affected by command construction, summarization, and retrieval distance thresholds.
